title: Odes 1.11: the 'carpe diem' ode and this translation
short: Eight lines to Leuconoe: stop consulting astrologers about death, accept what comes, and seize the day. Conington uses long trochaic couplets.
body: Odes 1.11 is one of Horace's shortest odes and the source of the phrase carpe diem. The speaker tells Leuconoe not to ask the astrologers how long they will live, to accept whatever comes, and to make the most of today. The metre is the greater Asclepiad, a long line built round three choriambs, which Horace also uses in Odes 1.18 and 4.10. Conington (translation first published 1863) renders it in rhymed couplets of long trochaic lines, the metre of Tennyson's 'Locksley Hall'. Some lines are so long that the archive text wraps them.

title: '('tis forbidden knowledge)'
short: Nefas, 'unlawful in the sight of the gods': it is impious to know the future, not just impossible.
body: The Latin is tu ne quaesieris, scire nefas, quem mihi, quem tibi / finem di dederint, 'do not ask (it is wrong to know) what end the gods have given me, what end you'. Nefas means what is forbidden by divine law, and Shorey translates scire nefas as ''tis wrong to know'. He notes that ne with the perfect subjunctive (quaesieris) is a sharper, more colloquial prohibition than the usual polite forms. Conington's parenthesis keeps the aside, and 'forbidden knowledge' brings in a faintly biblical sense of the fruit of knowledge.

title: 'what our destined term of years, / Mine and yours'
greek: quem mihi, quem tibi / finem di dederint
short: The 'end' (finis) the gods have set for each: the question is how long each of the two will live.
body: Horace asks quem mihi, quem tibi / finem di dederint, 'what end the gods have given to me, what end to you'. The repeated quem sets the two lives side by side, and the perfect dederint shows that the end is already fixed. Conington's 'destined term of years' paraphrases finem, making it a span rather than a final point. His 'Mine and yours' keeps the Latin's balance. Shorey's note collects other places where Horace says it is forbidden to know the future.

title: 'the tables of your Babylonish seers'
short: Babylonian 'numbers': the calculations of Chaldean astrologers, fashionable in Rome in Horace's day.
body: The Latin is nec Babylonios / temptaris numeros, 'and do not try Babylonian numbers'. Shorey explains numeros as the calculations of the Chaldean astrologers, called mathematici at Rome. He compares Tacitus, Histories 1.22, on astrologers at the court of Otho. Astrology from Mesopotamia spread through the Hellenistic world and was popular, and periodically banned, in Rome. Merrill, commenting on Catullus 5, cites this line for the belief that exact numbers give power over a life. Conington's 'tables' (astrological charts) and 'Babylonish' (an archaic adjective, OED) make the practice sound foreign and quaint.

title: Leuconoe
short: A Greek name, probably invented, meaning something like 'white-' or 'clear-minded'; its point is disputed.
body: Leuconoe is otherwise unknown and probably fictitious, like most of the names in the Odes. It is formed from Greek leukos ('white, bright') and noos ('mind'). Scholars disagree about the point: it may suggest a bright or innocent mind, or, ironically, an empty or simple one, in a woman who worries over horoscopes. Some have also connected the name with Leuconoe, one of the daughters of Minyas in Ovid's Metamorphoses. Conington's 'my Leuconoe' supplies a possessive that the Latin lacks and makes the poem more intimate.

anchor: Better far to bear the future
title: 'Better far to bear the future ... like the past'
short: 'How much better to endure whatever will be': acceptance of the unknown future, a theme shared by Epicureans and Stoics.
body: The Latin is ut melius, quidquid erit, pati, 'how much better to endure whatever shall be'. Shorey compares Aeneid 5.710, where all fortune is to be overcome by bearing it. Patience in the face of an unknown future was common ground for Epicurean and Stoic teaching, and Horace often presents the two together. Conington's 'like the past' is his own addition, which suggests that the future, once lived, will be no more terrible than what is already behind. The ode turns from prohibition to positive advice at this point.

title: 'many winters yet to give, or this our last'
greek: seu pluris hiemes seu tribuit Iuppiter ultimam
short: Years are counted in winters, which suits the stormy seascape of the next line.
body: The Latin is seu pluris hiemes seu tribuit Iuppiter ultimam, 'whether Jupiter has granted more winters, or this as the last'. Shorey notes that years are marked by winters or summers 'to suit the rhetorical color'. Here winter suits the scene of storm at sea that follows. He glosses tribuit as 'has assigned', like the Greek verbs for the Fates spinning a lot. Conington keeps 'winters', and 'Jove' for Iuppiter, and his 'this our last' makes the present winter possibly the final one.

title: 'the Tyrrhene billows'
greek: quae nunc oppositis debilitat pumicibus mare / Tyrrhenum
short: The Tyrrhenian Sea, off the west coast of Italy, breaking its winter waves on the porous rocks of the shore.
body: The Latin is quae nunc oppositis debilitat pumicibus mare / Tyrrhenum, 'which now wears out the Tyrrhenian sea on the rocks set against it'. The Tyrrhenian Sea lies between the west coast of Italy and Sardinia and Corsica. Shorey glosses debilitat as 'breaks the force of' and pumicibus as any wave-eaten, porous rock, comparing Lucretius. The line is often read as an image of time wearing everything down, or of the speaker and Leuconoe watching a winter storm from a villa by the sea. Conington's capitalised 'THIS' insists on the present winter.

title: 'Strain your wine and prove your wisdom'
short: Be wise and strain the wine: practical wisdom and a household task, filtering wine through cloth before drinking.
body: The Latin is sapias, vina liques, 'be wise, strain the wine'. Shorey glosses liques as straining wine through a cloth or strainer (colum) to clear it of sediment, a step in preparing it for drinking. The pairing makes wisdom concrete and domestic. Sapere ('to be wise') also originally means 'to taste', a link some readers hear here. Conington's 'prove your wisdom' adds 'prove', making it a test, where Horace gives a bare imperative.

title: 'life is short; should hope be more?'
short: 'Since life's span is short, cut back long hope': reseces is a vine-dresser's word for pruning; Conington turns it into a question.
body: The Latin is spatio brevi / spem longam reseces, 'and since the span is short, prune back long hope'. Shorey takes spatio brevi as 'life's span being short' and spem longam as hopes that look far into the future. He quotes Cowley's version: 'from a short life cut off all hopes that grow too long'. Resecare is used of cutting back vines, so the imagery anticipates carpe ('pluck') in the last line. Conington's rhetorical question 'should hope be more?' gives the sense but loses the pruning image.

title: 'In the moment of our talking, envious time has ebb'd away'
short: 'While we talk, envious time will have fled': the future perfect makes the loss already complete.
body: The Latin is dum loquimur, fugerit invida / aetas, 'while we speak, envious time will have fled'. Shorey glosses fugerit as 'will be gone' and collects parallels from Persius, Boileau and Milton ('Fly, envious Time'). Time is invida because it grudges men their happiness. The future perfect fugerit makes the passing complete even as it is described, so the poem enacts its own point: speaking about time uses it up. Conington's 'ebb'd away' takes up the sea imagery of line 5, a good touch, but turns the future perfect into a simple past.

title: 'Seize the present': carpe diem
short: Carpe means 'pluck, gather' like fruit or flowers; 'seize' is the common English rendering but loses the image of harvest.
body: Carpe diem, quam minimum credula postero is the poem's last line. Carpere means to pick or pluck fruit or flowers, and so to enjoy something as it comes to hand. Shorey notes both senses, 'catch as it flies' and 'pluck the flower of', and a comparable use in Persius 5.151, carpamus dulcia ('let us pluck life's sweets'). The image completes the vine imagery of vina liques and reseces. Conington's 'Seize the present', like the familiar 'seize the day', stresses urgency rather than gathering. Carpe diem has become a general motto, and the Epicurean context (enjoy what is present, do not depend on the future) is often forgotten.

title: 'trust to-morrow e'en as little as you may'
short: 'Trusting the next day as little as possible': credula, feminine, is addressed to Leuconoe.
body: The final phrase quam minimum credula postero means 'trusting as little as possible in the following (day)'. Shorey supplies diei with postero. The feminine credula reminds us that the advice is to Leuconoe, who has been trusting astrologers. The same word credulus is used of Pyrrha's naive lover in Odes 1.5. Shorey quotes FitzGerald's Omar Khayyam on tomorrow. Conington's 'e'en as little as you may' is an accurate version of quam minimum, though slower than the Latin.
